lesson.title: Introduction to Discussion Text
lesson.content: A Discussion Text is a text which presents a problematic discourse. This problem will be discussed from different points of view. It is commonly found in philosophical, historic, and social texts. The social function is to present (at least) two points of view about an issue. It consists of: Statement of Issue, List of Supporting Points (Pros), List of Contrastive Points (Cons), and Conclusion/Recommendation.

lesson.title: Structure: The Statement of Issue
lesson.content: The first paragraph of a discussion text introduces the topic and why it is being discussed. It usually presents a question or a statement that highlights the controversy. For example, 'The use of artificial intelligence in education has sparked a heated debate among experts and parents alike.' This sets the stage for the arguments that follow.

lesson.title: Presenting Supporting Points (Pros)
lesson.content: After stating the issue, the writer presents the 'Arguments For'. Each point should be supported by evidence or explanation. Common transition words include: 'Proponents argue...', 'One advantage is...', 'On the positive side...'. For instance, in a discussion about remote work, a supporting point would be the flexibility it offers to employees.

lesson.title: Presenting Contrastive Points (Cons)
lesson.content: The 'Arguments Against' provide the opposing view. This is crucial for balance. Use transition words like: 'However...', 'On the other hand...', 'Critics claim...'. In the remote work example, a contrastive point might be the lack of face-to-face social interaction and potential for blurred boundaries between work and home life.

lesson.title: Language Features: Contrastive Conjunctions
lesson.content: Discussion texts rely heavily on conjunctions to show relationship between ideas. 1. Additive: 'In addition', 'Furthermore'. 2. Contrastive: 'In contrast', 'Conversely', 'Nevertheless'. 3. Causal: 'Therefore', 'Consequently'. These words help the reader follow the transition from one side of the debate to the other.

lesson.title: Conclusion and Recommendation
lesson.content: The final part summarizes the arguments and presents the writer's own stance or a balanced recommendation. It doesn't necessarily have to pick a side but should provide a logical closure. Examples: 'In conclusion, while there are risks, the benefits outweigh them if managed properly' or 'Therefore, a middle-ground approach is suggested'.

lesson.title: Introduction to Review Text
lesson.content: A Review Text is an evaluation of a publication, service, or company such as a movie, video game, musical composition, book, or a piece of hardware. Its purpose is to summarize, analyze, and assess the merit of the work. The structure usually includes: Introduction (Orientation), Evaluation (Interpretative Recount), and Summary (Evaluation/Critique).

lesson.title: Orientation and Context
lesson.content: The orientation provides the background information about the work being reviewed. This includes the title, the author/creator, the genre, and a brief overview of the plot or purpose. It sets the scene for the reader so they know exactly what is being evaluated. For a movie, this would include the director and lead actors.

lesson.title: The Interpretative Recount (Plot Summary)
lesson.content: This section provides a summary of the work. It should highlight the key events or features without giving away spoilers. The focus is on providing enough detail so the reader understands the context of the evaluation that follows. It's about 'what happens' in the book or movie.

lesson.title: Evaluation: Analyzing Strengths and Weaknesses
lesson.content: This is the core of the review. The reviewer analyzes specific elements like acting, cinematography, writing style, or functionality. Use descriptive adjectives (e.g., 'gripping', 'tedious', 'innovative', 'derivative'). A good review balances positive and negative aspects to provide a fair assessment.

lesson.title: Summarizing and Final Verdict
lesson.content: The conclusion restates the reviewer's overall opinion. It often includes a recommendation—whether the reader should see the movie, read the book, or buy the product. Phrases like 'Overall, I would highly recommend...', 'Fans of the genre will enjoy...', or 'It’s not worth the hype' are common here.

lesson.title: Language Features: Evaluative Language
lesson.content: Review texts use specific language features: 1. Present tense (usually). 2. Focusing on specific participants. 3. Using adjectives and adverbs of quality. 4. Using metaphors or idioms to express opinion (e.g., 'a roller-coaster of emotions', 'fell flat'). This helps convey the reviewer's subjective experience in an engaging way.

lesson.title: Introduction to Subjunctive and Wish
lesson.content: The subjunctive mood and the verb 'wish' are used to express hypothetical situations, desires, or things that are contrary to fact. They are often used to talk about things we want to be different from reality. Common patterns include 'I wish...', 'If only...', or expressions like 'It is vital that...'.

lesson.title: Wishing for the Present
lesson.content: To express a wish about a present situation that we are unhappy with, we use 'wish' + Simple Past. Formula: Subject + wish + Subject + V2 (Past). Example: 'I wish I had a car' (Reality: I don't have a car). 'I wish I were taller' (Note: 'were' is used for all persons, including I, he, she, it).

lesson.title: Wishing for the Past (Regrets)
lesson.content: To express a wish or regret about a past situation, we use 'wish' + Past Perfect. Formula: Subject + wish + Subject + had + V3. Example: 'I wish I had studied harder for the test' (Reality: I didn't study hard). 'I wish she hadn't left so early' (Reality: She left early).

lesson.title: Wishing for the Future / Change in Behavior
lesson.content: To express a desire for someone's behavior to change or for something to happen in the future, we use 'wish' + would. Formula: Subject + wish + Subject + would + V1. Example: 'I wish it would stop raining', 'I wish you would listen to me'. This often implies annoyance or impatience.

lesson.title: Formal Subjunctive: Suggestions and Necessity
lesson.content: In formal English, the subjunctive is used after verbs like 'suggest', 'recommend', 'insist', 'demand'. Formula: Verb + that + Subject + Base Form (V1). Example: 'The doctor suggested that he quit smoking' (not 'quits'). 'It is essential that she be present at the meeting' (not 'is').

lesson.title: Practice: Reality vs. Wish
lesson.content: Practice converting reality to wish sentences. Reality: 'I am poor.' -> Wish: 'I wish I were rich.' Reality: 'He didn't come.' -> Wish: 'I wish he had come.' Reality: 'You are making too much noise.' -> Wish: 'I wish you would be quiet.' Identifying the time (present, past, or future) is the first step.

lesson.title: TOEFL Structure: Subjects and Verbs
lesson.content: One of the most common errors in the TOEFL Structure section is missing subjects or verbs. Every sentence in English must have at least one subject and one verb. Watch out for 'extra' words like prepositional phrases that might distract you from the true subject. Example: 'The boy (S) always (Adv) plays (V) soccer'.

lesson.title: TOEFL Structure: Parallelism
lesson.content: Parallel structure means using the same pattern of words to show that two or more ideas have the same level of importance. This often occurs with 'and', 'but', 'or'. Example: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and biking' (all -ing). Incorrect: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike'. Check for consistency in verb tenses and word forms.

lesson.title: TOEFL Reading: Main Idea Questions
lesson.content: Reading passages always have a primary focus. Main idea questions ask you to identify the central theme. Tip: Read the first and last sentences of each paragraph. They often contain the topic sentence. Look for answer choices that summarize the whole passage, not just one specific detail.

lesson.title: TOEFL Reading: Vocabulary in Context
lesson.content: You will be asked to find the meaning of a word as it is used in the passage. Don't rely solely on your memory of the word; look at the surrounding sentences for clues (context). Synonyms, antonyms, or examples nearby can help you deduce the meaning. Replace the word in the sentence with the options to see which fits best.

lesson.title: TOEFL Reading: Scanning for Details
lesson.content: Detail questions ask for specific facts. Use 'scanning'—moving your eyes quickly over the text to find keywords from the question (names, dates, specific nouns). Once you find the keyword, read the sentence carefully to find the answer. Be careful with 'Not' or 'Except' questions which require finding what is NOT mentioned.

lesson.title: Time Management Strategies
lesson.content: TOEFL is a timed test. In the Reading section, don't spend too long on one question; if you're stuck, guess and move on. In the Structure section, practice identifying sentence patterns quickly. Efficiency is just as important as accuracy. Aim to spend about 1-1.5 minutes per reading question.

lesson.title: Introducing Yourself Professionally
lesson.content: The most common opening question is 'Tell me about yourself'. This is not about your personal life, but your professional journey. Use the 'Present-Past-Future' formula: what you do now, your relevant background/education, and why you are excited about this specific opportunity. Keep it under 2 minutes.

lesson.title: Talking About Strengths and Weaknesses
lesson.content: When asked about strengths, provide specific examples (e.g., 'I am highly organized; in my last project I...'). For weaknesses, pick a real but minor technical skill and explain how you are improving it (e.g., 'I used to struggle with public speaking, but I've taken a course and recently led a group presentation').

lesson.title: Handling Situational Questions (STAR Method)
lesson.content: Questions like 'Tell me about a time you faced a challenge' should be answered using the STAR method: 1. Situation: Set the scene. 2. Task: What was the goal? 3. Action: What did YOU specifically do? 4. Result: What was the positive outcome? This provides a clear, structured, and evidence-based answer.

lesson.title: Common Interview Vocabulary
lesson.content: Use professional 'power verbs': 'coordinated', 'implemented', 'facilitated', 'initiated', 'resolved'. Avoid 'I just did...', use 'I was responsible for...'. Understand terms like 'KPIs', 'team-oriented', 'deadline-driven', and 'proactive'. Using the right industry terminology shows you are prepared and knowledgeable.

lesson.title: Asking Smart Questions to the Interviewer
lesson.content: At the end, always have questions ready. It shows interest. Examples: 'What does a typical day look like in this role?', 'How would you describe the company culture?', 'What are the biggest challenges the team is currently facing?'. Avoid asking about salary or benefits in the first interview unless the employer brings it up.

lesson.title: Body Language and Soft Skills
lesson.content: It's not just what you say, but how you say it. Maintain eye contact, sit up straight, and smile. Use active listening—nod and use fillers like 'I see' or 'That's interesting'. In a virtual interview, look at the camera, not the screen. Punctuality, professional attire, and a firm handshake (or polite greeting) are non-verbal cues of competence.
